title: What is the difference between an idempotent producer and a transactional producer?

s1_definition.profdef: An idempotent producer guarantees that retries never create duplicate records within a single producer session on a single partition; Kafka deduplicates using a producer id and per-partition sequence numbers. A transactional producer builds on top of idempotence and adds atomic, all-or-nothing writes across multiple partitions and topics, plus the ability to atomically commit consumed offsets together with produced records. An idempotent producer prevents duplicates from retries; a transactional producer additionally makes a group of writes commit or abort as one unit that consumers can be configured to read only when committed.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of Rajesh sending a transfer instruction to the bank. An idempotent producer is like each instruction having a unique serial number, so if Rajesh's phone retries on a timeout, the bank sees the same serial and records it only once — no accidental double transfer. A transactional producer is like a notary who wraps several instructions into one sealed envelope: either all of them are filed together or none are, and clerks can be told to ignore envelopes that were never sealed. Idempotence stops one instruction being counted twice; transactions make a whole batch of instructions atomic.
s1_definition.oneliner: Idempotence stops retry duplicates on one partition in one session; transactions add atomic all-or-nothing writes across many partitions plus atomic read-process-write with offsets.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An idempotent producer guarantees that retries never create duplicate records within a single producer session on a single partition; Kafka deduplicates using a producer id and per-partition sequence numbers. A transactional producer builds on top of idempotence and adds atomic, all-or-nothing writes across multiple partitions and topics, plus the ability to atomically commit consumed offsets together with produced records. An idempotent producer prevents duplicates from retries; a transactional producer additionally makes a group of writes commit or abort as one unit that consumers can be configured to read only when committed.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of Rajesh sending a transfer instruction to the bank. An idempotent producer is like each instruction having a unique serial number, so if Rajesh's phone retries on a timeout, the bank sees the same serial and records it only once — no accidental double transfer. A transactional producer is like a notary who wraps several instructions into one sealed envelope: either all of them are filed together or none are, and clerks can be told to ignore envelopes that were never sealed. Idempotence stops one instruction being counted twice; transactions make a whole batch of instructions atomic.

**One line to remember:** Idempotence stops retry duplicates on one partition in one session; transactions add atomic all-or-nothing writes across many partitions plus atomic read-process-write with offsets.

sections.s2_technical:
The idempotent producer solves a narrow but critical problem. When a producer sends a record and the broker writes it but the acknowledgement is lost on the network, the producer retries, and without idempotence that retry becomes a duplicate. With idempotence enabled, the broker assigns the producer a unique producer id and tracks a sequence number per partition. If it sees a record whose sequence it has already written, it acknowledges it again but does not write it twice. You enable it with `enable.idempotence=true`, which is actually the default in recent Kafka, and it requires `acks=all`, `retries` greater than zero, and `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` at most five. The guarantee is scoped to one producer session and per partition, so it protects against retry duplicates, not against application-level resends or writes spanning partitions.

The transactional producer is a superset. It requires a `transactional.id`, which lets Kafka fence out a previous instance of the same producer so a zombie cannot keep writing after a new instance starts. You call `initTransactions()` once, then wrap work in `beginTransaction()`, one or more `send()` calls that may target several partitions and topics, and either `commitTransaction()` or `abortTransaction()`. All records in the transaction become visible together or not at all. Crucially, a transactional producer can also call `sendOffsetsToTransaction()` to commit the consumer offsets for what it just read inside the same transaction, which is the foundation of exactly-once stream processing in a consume-process-produce loop.

Consumers participate through `isolation.level`. With `read_committed`, a consumer only sees records from committed transactions and skips aborted ones, waiting at the last stable offset for in-flight transactions to resolve. With the default `read_uncommitted`, it sees everything immediately. So transactions only deliver their guarantee end to end when consumers read committed.

The senior nuances are these. Idempotence is cheap and should essentially always be on, because it removes a whole class of silent duplicate bugs for free. Transactions add real cost: a two-phase commit coordinated through a transaction coordinator, extra latency, and transaction markers written to the log. So I use transactions only where atomicity across multiple writes or exactly-once read-process-write is a genuine requirement, such as debiting one account topic and crediting another in one atomic step, and I rely on plain idempotence everywhere else. In Spring Kafka, setting a `transactionIdPrefix` on the producer factory turns the `KafkaTemplate` transactional and lets you use `executeInTransaction` or the `@Transactional` annotation with the Kafka transaction manager.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India produces transfer events and occasionally the network drops the acknowledgement, so the producer retries. Without protection, a single transfer event appears twice on the topic and the downstream ledger double-counts it. This is exactly what the idempotent producer prevents: the broker sees the same sequence number and writes the record only once.

Problem 2 — A money movement must write a debit event to the accounts topic and a credit event to the ledger topic, and these must both appear or neither. If the process crashes after the debit but before the credit, consumers must never see a lonely debit. This is exactly what the transactional producer provides: both sends are wrapped in one transaction that commits atomically, and read-committed consumers only see them once committed.

We simulate both in plain Java. An `IdempotentBroker` tracks per-partition sequence numbers and ignores duplicates. A `TransactionalBroker` buffers sends and only makes them visible on commit, discarding them on abort. The demo retries a send to show deduplication, then runs a debit-plus-credit transaction with a commit and with an abort. The code will show: a `Record` holder, the two broker simulators, and a demo covering retry dedup, commit, and abort.

```yaml
# application.yml — idempotent + transactional producer in Spring Kafka
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    producer:
      acks: all
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
        max.in.flight.requests.per.connection: 5
      transaction-id-prefix: tx-settlement-   # makes KafkaTemplate transactional
    consumer:
      isolation-level: read_committed          # only see committed transactions
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one transfer event sent twice due to a retry, then a debit-plus-credit pair committed, then a debit aborted.

Step 1: The idempotent broker receives the transfer with sequence 100 on partition 3 and writes it, recording that the last sequence for that partition is 100.

Step 2: The acknowledgement is lost, so the producer retries the identical record with sequence 100. The broker sees 100 is not greater than the last written 100, so it acknowledges but does not store a second copy. The log still holds exactly one record.

Step 3: The transactional broker begins a transaction and buffers a debit on the accounts topic and a credit on the ledger topic. Neither is visible yet because the transaction is still open.

Step 4: The producer commits. Both the debit and the credit move into the committed log together, so a read-committed consumer now sees both at once, never one without the other.

Step 5: A second transaction buffers a debit, then the process simulates a crash and aborts. The buffered debit is discarded, so the committed log is unchanged and read-committed consumers never see the lonely debit.

```
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ] First send stored=true, retry stored=false, log size=1
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ] After COMMIT, read_committed sees 2 records.
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [WARNING] Crash before credit -> abort transaction
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ] After ABORT, read_committed STILL sees 2 records (lonely debit never appeared).
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  IDEMPOTENT PRODUCER
  send(transfer, seq=100) ──→ broker writes, lastSeq=100
  (ack lost) retry seq=100 ──→ broker: 100 <= 100 → ACK but NO duplicate
                                        │
                                        ▼  log has exactly 1 record

  TRANSACTIONAL PRODUCER
  beginTransaction()
    │ send(DEBIT accounts)   ─┐ buffered, NOT visible
    │ send(CREDIT ledger)    ─┘
    ├─ commitTransaction() ──→ both appear together ─→ read_committed sees 2
    └─ abortTransaction()  ──→ all discarded ────────→ read_committed sees nothing extra
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
An idempotent producer and a transactional producer solve two different reliability problems, and the transactional one is a superset of the idempotent one. The idempotent producer fixes the duplicate-from-retry problem. When the broker writes a record but the acknowledgement is lost, the producer retries, and without idempotence that becomes a duplicate. With idempotence on, the broker assigns a producer id and tracks a sequence number per partition, so if it sees a sequence it has already written, it acknowledges again but does not store a second copy. It needs acks all, retries above zero, and at most five in-flight requests, and it is the default now because it removes a whole class of silent duplicate bugs essentially for free. Its scope is one producer session and one partition.

The transactional producer builds on idempotence and adds atomicity across many partitions and topics. It requires a transactional id, which lets Kafka fence out a previous zombie instance of the same producer. You call init once, then wrap work in begin, several sends, and either commit or abort, and all those records become visible together or not at all. Critically, it can also commit the consumer offsets for what it just read inside the same transaction, which is how exactly-once consume-process-produce works. Consumers only get the guarantee if they read with isolation level read-committed, which skips aborted and in-flight records.

The way I decide between them is by cost and need. Idempotence is cheap, so it is on everywhere. Transactions add a real two-phase commit through a transaction coordinator, extra latency, and transaction markers in the log, so I reserve them for cases that genuinely need atomicity across writes or exactly-once processing, like debiting one topic and crediting another as one unit so consumers never see a lonely debit.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, every producer runs idempotent so a retried transfer event is never double-counted in the ledger. For actual money movement that spans a debit topic and a credit topic, we use a transactional producer with a transaction id prefix on the Kafka template, wrap the debit and credit in one transaction, and run the downstream ledger consumers with read-committed so a crash between the debit and the credit leaves nothing visible rather than a dangling debit. The senior framing I give is that idempotence is table stakes for correctness under retries, while transactions are a deliberate, more expensive tool you apply precisely where all-or-nothing semantics are a hard business requirement.
